claims.text: Adding or increasing Cr and Ta in a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote formation of a CrTaO4-based oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.
A CrTaO4-based oxide layer can improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The protective CrTaO4-based oxide scale will be continuous.
The protective CrTaO4-based oxide scale will be adherent.
Added Cr and Ta preferentially oxidize to form a stable CrTaO4-based scale.
The CrTaO4-based scale acts as a diffusion barrier that slows oxygen transport into the alloy.
Formation of the protective scale reduces continued oxidation and degradation of the underlying alloy.
The modified alloy will have significantly lower oxidation weight gain than a comparable alloy without the Cr and Ta adjustment.
Lower oxidation weight gain indicates improved oxygen resistance.
An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed at 1100 °C in air develops a non-protective scale and shows exponential weight gain.
A dense protective CrTaO4-based scale can form on a refractory high-entropy alloy at 1100 °C during exposure lasting up to 200 hours.
The CrTaO4-based protective mechanism operates under an air atmosphere.
Cr and Ta concentrations must exceed a critical threshold for continuous CrTaO4 formation.
Failure to form a dense or coherent CrTaO4-based scale prevents the expected oxidation-resistance improvement.
The precise critical Cr and Ta concentrations required for protection are not established.
The quantitative magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement remains to be experimentally validated.
Failure either to form CrTaO4 on the modified alloy or to obtain significantly lower weight gain than the control would falsify the hypothesis.
